title: The Coming Revolution in Art History Teaching
author: David Carrier
content:
![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/A_Google_Glass_wearer-680x453.jpg)

Photograph Source: Loïc Le Meur - Flickr: Loïc Le Meur - [CC BY
2.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/)

Welcome freshman! This is your introduction to art history class. Please
unpack your Google glasses and charge them up. And check the plane tickets,
which will take you to China, Egypt, Italy, and India, and also France, New
York, and South America. To study art history, travel is necessary. (And
fortunately ours is a very well-endowed university.) You will have an exciting
semester!

When you visit these great art historical sites, you will use your Google
glasses to read the commentaries the faculty have assembled while looking at
the artworks. As you view this art, you can view these learned commentaries at
the same time. And so, you are in the right position to check whether these
written accounts are correct. What has always defined art history, for the
ancients as in the Renaissance and up to the late twentieth century, is that
there is a distance between art writing and the visual artifacts that it
describes. Whether we’re concerned with the readers of Vasari, who took his
printed texts on their travels in Italy; with the readers of Baudelaire, who
carried his Salons to the French galleries; or the Americans who hefted
Clement Greenberg’s collected essays into American museums.

This tradition remains of live importance. When I was writing my book on
Neapolitan baroque churches, I carried the commentaries into the pew, and
turned from one to the next, from text to image, moving back and forth between
reading and looking. Now, however, that gap in experience has been eliminated.
You can see imposed on the art the commentary about it. In my books in
progress on Naples, and more recently, on Venice, I have found the vast array
of YouTube materials online immensely helpful. San Marco is a very complicated
and looking just at the isolated images, it’s extremely difficult to get a
feel for the organization of the whole. How helpful it would be to have a
model presenting the organization of all these images. Already, you can
refresh your memory of the setting of nearly every church and almost all
paintings by looking at the YouTube commentaries. Designed often for touristic
purposes, they provide very valuable information for the art historian. And
now the materials in this class develop that way of thinking. Obviously this
procedure doesn’t solve all of our interpretative problems. The analysis you
are reading may be misleading, mistaken or even entirely wrongheaded. But the
elimination of any gap between the interpretation and what we are seeing
surely makes it easier to identify problems. If there is a discrepancy between
what you read and what you see, then you know that the problem lies with the
text, which is not inaccurate.

+++

This pedagogic novelty is, I regret to say, is still just a fantasy. So far as
I know, no such classes are as yet being conducted. And I have not yet seen
the Google Glass technology, which is still expensive. The reported worry was
that using these glasses would eliminate privacy. But all of the necessary
technology is, so I believe, at hand. And in Naples, at the display of
Caravaggio’s Seven Acts of Mercy already a couple of years ago there was a
primitive version of this computer technology. And so I am almost certain that
better versions will very soon appear. The matching of text to picture is such
a basic art historical concern that the computer technology is sure to be
developed.

Currently I am much concerned with Giorgione’s The Tempest (1507), which is in
the Academy in Venice. The basic scholarly dilemma involves asking what
interpretation can describe the man, the woman, the child, and the landscape.
This picture looks simple, and so very many competing interpretations are
proposed. Maybe it is a scene from Scripture; perhaps it depicts contemporary
political events; possibly it is a free play of fantasy. In your study, you
can consult Salvatore Settis’ _Giorgione 's Tempest: Interpreting the Hidden
Subject_, which lists 38 interpretations. How helpful it would be to read all
of those accounts in the museum gallery while looking directly at the
painting.

Here I have only considered the viewpoint of my students, whose experience of
art museums will be dramatically changed. But what about art history research-
-how will it be affected? Just as the replacement of internal combustion
engines by electric motors is about to change how automobiles look, are
manufactured, and are maintained, so I expect that these new technologies will
transform how we understand visual art. This will be an exciting moment, if
only we scholars can get financial support for our research. Recently, the
ready availability of high-quality images online has changed the everyday
practice of art history writing. And so I believe that other potentially
beneficial changes are sure now to come quickly.
